title: Syllabus
text:
I am an R enthusiast! At times this course will be challenging, but I promise you the hard work will pay off. Please read this document fully. You may post questions on Piazza or bring them to our first class on 9/1.
R is the standard tool for performing statistics in biology, health studies, data science, and many other fields. Because of this, B215 is neither just a biostatistics course nor simply an R programming course: it is a biostatistics course where R is directly integrated into the learning process. Throughout the course, we use motivating case studies and data analysis problem sets and R labs based on similar challenges to those one finds in scientific research.

title: Syllabus
text:
Late work
If you anticipate being unable to attend a meeting, please contact me as soon as possible as your circumstances allow. Note that problem sets are due in class (hard copy) so if you miss class you must make arrangements to have this handed in on time. It is your responsibility to gather class notes from classmates and complete any missed activities that may not be in the schedule. These make-up materials should be submitted within 3 days of your absence (unless otherwise negotiated; for longer absences or extenuating circumstances, please contact me to work something out). Sick days do not count as unexcused absences! Just let me know ASAP.
The course is structured in such a way that you can have some late work without penalty. So there will be no make-up assignments.
Grace days. Each student may use up to 4 “grace days” during the semester to hand in work late, no questions asked and without penalty. To use your grace day(s) for an assignment, email me at least a day before the assignment is due and communicate how many grace days you are requesting. There is no need to provide any explanation as to why you are using your grace days; as long as you have enough days left in the semester to use, and have written to me at least a day in advance, I will approve. You can use grace days for any assignments except for your final coding project, exams, and the peer-review activity.
Outside of the grace days, I will accept late work with a reduction in grade as follows: if you turn in the work 1 minute to 24h late, your maximum score will drop to 90%; if you turn it in 24h and 1 minute to 48h late, it will drop to 80%; and so on. Late lecture quizzes and DataCamp will be accepted anytime without penalty but I strongly urge you to keep up with the work. Note that you can retake the lecture quizzes as many times as you want. I am only grading whether or not you did it.
If you are dealing with an emergency or other issue and believe you may require more leniency, please email me and your dean as soon as possible so that we can make arrangements.

title: Syllabus
text:
Plagiarism
All students enrolled in Bryn Mawr Classes are bound by the The Bryn Mawr honor code. I call your attention to the sections on plagiarism and AI use in the code, which will be followed here. Contributions from “outside sources”, including AI sources, must be properly quoted and cited every time they are used. Outside sources include content that was produced by a genAI assistant like ChatGPT, Gemini, and others. Failure to do so constitutes an academic integrity violation, in accordance with the College’s Honor Code:

“In reports and other written work, sources of information and of ideas and opinions not the student’s own must be clearly indicated; the source of direct quotations must be acknowledged. Failure to do so constitutes plagiarism (…) Generative AI tools should not be used in the completion of any course assignments, exams, or written work, including laboratory work, unless an instructor for a given course has specifically and explicitly authorized their use for the assignment in question. (…) Presenting AI-generated content as original student work, submitting AI-generated content without citing its source in artificial intelligence tools, and relying on generative AI tools for closed-book quizzes, tests, and exams all constitute violations of the Honor Code.” – BMC Honor Code2

I will call out code that looks vibe-coded in your assignments. Please don’t do it.
All work submitted in this course must be your own. In plain words: do not use genAI to write any of your answers to prompts, problems, and do not submit any prose generated by genAI. You may of course use genAI to study, but do so at your own peril, as I expect your work do reflect the content from the course and I do not authorize the materials from this course to be fed to LLMs. You may use genAI to help you brainstorm/define concepts but if you do so, you must attribute properly. Similarly, if your discussions with classmates informed how you answered any of the questions, you must give them proper attribution.
You may use LLMs/GenAI for coding assignments ONLY, and only in certain ways 3:

to brainstorm ideas
to decode cryptic error messages or explain why they might have occurred
to ask specific questions about R-language related things like function parameters, etc.

If you do use LLMs for the coding assignment, you must include citations for each instance where you used it, including the prompt you used (I will provide more specific guidelines with the assignments themselves).
For problem sets and other assignments: You may not use AI, as there is no (ethical) reason to do so. The whole point of these formative assessments is to learn and/or practice for the exams.
If I suspect these guidelines have been violated, I will call the student over to discuss their process in generating the content.

title: 1.2.Random samples, sampling error and bias, accuracy and precision
text:
Quick recap
Last lecture we introduced:

Population vs. sample
Parameter vs. estimate
The two types of errors associated with sampling: sampling error and sampling bias

Ask for volunteers to remind these concepts

title: 1.2.Random samples, sampling error and bias, accuracy and precision
text:
Statistics three broad goals:

Estimation: estimate the values of important parameters and have measures of uncertainty for estimates
Hypothesis testing: Test hypotheses about those parameters
Causal inference: Teasing apart causation from correlation

Statistics claims to be obsessed with the TRUTH. It’s meant to be a way of understanding the world. It’s meant to describe and differentiate, and ideally, to tease apart causation from correlation. These three goals of statistics (below) are the beams of light we, as statisticians, try to shine on questions. That is – these three things are what you call a statistician to do.

title: 1.2.Random samples, sampling error and bias, accuracy and precision
text:
Learning Goals

Identify the properties of a good sample
Distinguish between sampling bias and sampling error.
Identify why estimates from samples may deviate from parameters of populations
Distinguish between accuracy and precision and how these terms relate to sampling bias and sampling error.

title: 1.2.Random samples, sampling error and bias, accuracy and precision
text:
Properties of a good sample

Random


Equality: probability of being selected reflects its representation in the population
Independence: no influence of sampling one individual on other individuals that get sampled.


A sufficiently large number of individuals.

title: 1.2.Random samples, sampling error and bias, accuracy and precision
text:
Random samples

Taking random samples is hard and requires effort


Why are they important? Reduce sampling bias
How to get a random sample (ideal):

Carefully characterize a population and use computer code to select participants randomly.

text: Probability Distribution vs. Frequency Distribution

title: 1.2.Random samples, sampling error and bias, accuracy and precision
text:
Example




Probability distribution: The proportion of the population with a given value (often approximated with a function)




Frequency distribution: The number of times a value occurs in a sample.



Hide the codeplot.one.dice.prob <- data.frame(outcome = c(1:6), probability = 1/6) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = outcome, y = probability, fill = factor(outcome))) +
    geom_bar(stat = "identity", show.legend = FALSE) + ggtitle("Probability Distribution",
    subtitle = "Outcome of a fair die") + scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:6) +
    scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0), limits = c(0, 0.32)) +
    ylab("Expected probability") + theme(axis.ticks = element_blank())
df <- data.frame(Outcome = DieRoll(times = 6), NrRolls = 6)

one.roll <- ggplot(df, aes(x = Outcome, fill = factor(Outcome))) +
    geom_bar(aes(y = after_stat(count)/sum(count)), show.legend = FALSE) +
    ggtitle("Proportions Observed", subtitle = "Outcome of a fair die\n(n = 6 trials)") +
    # scale_fill_manual(values = banff())+
scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:12) + ylab(label = "Observed proportion") +
    theme(axis.ticks = element_blank())
library(patchwork)
plot.one.dice.prob + one.roll

title: 1.2.Random samples, sampling error and bias, accuracy and precision
text:
Estimates are random variables

Because an estimate is a random variable, the value of an estimate is influenced by chance.


A random variable can take on many different values with different probabilities. Random variables are ways to map outcomes of random processes to numbers. – Khan Academy


Therefore estimates will differ among random samples from the same population.


we’re assuming here that we don’t have the bias issue discussed for this example previously.

title: 1.2.Random samples, sampling error and bias, accuracy and precision
text:
The major goals of sampling


minimize sampling error (increase precision of estimates)
minimize sampling bias (increase accuracy of estimates)


Sampling: What could go wrong? {visibility=“hidden”}

title: 1.2.Random samples, sampling error and bias, accuracy and precision
text:
Sampling error

Sampling error: Chance deviations between estimates and the truth due to chance/luck– even when you did NOTHING wrong!


Sampling error is the difference between the estimate and its true parameter value — and it can be quantified!

title: 1.2.Random samples, sampling error and bias, accuracy and precision
section: Sampling error and precision of an estimate
text:
Sampling error and precision of an estimate

The spread of estimates resulting from sampling error indicates the precision of an estimate.
The lower the sampling error, the higher the precision.
All else being equal, larger samples will have lower sampling error and higher precision than smaller samples.

title: 1.2.Random samples, sampling error and bias, accuracy and precision
text:
Example of sampling error

The parameter “probability of getting a 6” is 1/6 (~0.17). The observed proportion in six random die rolls here was 0.





In this context we can think of each trial (die roll) as a sample. So our sample size here is 6.

title: 1.2.Random samples, sampling error and bias, accuracy and precision
section: Sampling error declines with sample size
text: Sampling error declines with sample size

title: 1.2.Random samples, sampling error and bias, accuracy and precision
text:
Sampling bias



If you collected these against a dark background without careful procedures… 




This sample is biased. There is a higher proportion of orange stars than the population from which it was taken. Therefore, it is not a representative sample of the underlying population.

Sampling bias case study
Sampling bias: Systematic difference between parameters & estimates.

Case study: Polls in the 1936 US Election.

title: 1.2.Random samples, sampling error and bias, accuracy and precision
text:
Sampling Bias in the 1936 Polls!

Questionnaire was more likely to reach rich people (who could afford phones & attend book clubs) than those with fewer means.
Voting and party preference are correlated with wealth.
Poorer people (underrepresented in the poll) supported Roosevelt, carrying him to victory.

title: 1.2.Random samples, sampling error and bias, accuracy and precision
text:
Sample of convenience

A sample of convenience is a collection of individuals that happen to be available at the time

… usually one that is drawn from a source that is conveniently accessible to the researcher.


Andrade C (2021). The Inconvenient Truth About Convenience and Purposive Samples. Indian J Psychol Med, 43(1):86-88. DOI: 10.1177/0253717620977000

title: 1.2.Random samples, sampling error and bias, accuracy and precision
text:
Sample of convenience: Problems

low generalizability. What is true for your sample might not reflect what is true for the population.
a sample is likely to be representative of the population only if it is randomly drawn from the population – the sample of convenience violates this assumption (and sometimes also the independence assumption)
in practice, you can only generalize findings to the subpopulation from which the sample was taken from.

title: 1.2.Random samples, sampling error and bias, accuracy and precision
section: Sometimes a sample of convenience is our only option
text:
Sometimes a sample of convenience is our only option

A sample of convenience may be the best option researchers have (e.g. studies that extract data from national healthcare or insurance databases)
Note: It is rarely possible to draw a truly random sample from the population – but we must do our best.

This does not invalidate the studies in question. They can have high “internal validity”. The issue is with generalizing, i.e, its external validity.
However, this is possible only if our sample is representative of the population; a sample is likely to be representative of the population only if it is randomly drawn from the population.

title: 1.2.Random samples, sampling error and bias, accuracy and precision
text:
Selection bias

“Occurs when individuals or groups in a study differ systematically from the population of interest leading to a systematic error in an association or outcome.” – Catalog of Bias [https://catalogofbias.org/biases/selection-bias/]






From: https://xkcd.com/2618/. We carefully sampled the general population and found that most people are familiar with acquiescence bias.

title: 1.2.Random samples, sampling error and bias, accuracy and precision
text:
Volunteer bias

Volunteers for a study are likely to be different, on average, from the population. Also known as “self-selection” bias.

For example:

Volunteers for sex studies are more likely to be open about sex.
In surveys about sexual activity, gender biases answers in opposite directions.
Volunteers for medical studies may be sicker than the general population.
Animals that are caught may be slower or more docile than those that are not.
The case we saw about the 1936 U.S. elections.

Ask for volunteers to name some. The US elections example also involves sample of convenience.

title: 1.2.Random samples, sampling error and bias, accuracy and precision
section: How bias and sampling error affect estimates
text:
How bias and sampling error affect estimates
In summary



Sampling Bias



Systematic difference between estimates & parameters.
Driven by bias in the sampling process (i.e., sample not random in relation to the population of interest), regarless of sample size.



Sampling Error


Undirected deviation of estimates away from parameters.

Driven by chance.
Decreases with sample size.

title: 1.2.Random samples, sampling error and bias, accuracy and precision
text:
Goals of estimation: visual summary

Accuracy (on average gets the correct answer).


Precision (gives a similar answer repeatedly). If unbiased, those estimated are centered around the true value (parameter).


Image: Wikipedia Commons (public domain).

title: 01. R, Rstudio: Crash Course
text:
Numbers
There are three number types in R:

numeric: the most common type in R; contains any number with or without a decimal
integer: numeric data without decimals. This is used when you are certain that you will never create a variable that should contain decimals. Just add the letter L after the number to create an integer.
complex: number is written with an “i” as the imaginary part. Less used.

title: 01. R, Rstudio: Crash Course
text:
Example
Try these in the sandbox at the end of this section.
x <- 200.8  # numeric
y <- 1000L  # integer
z <- 1i     # complex
Try these, one at a time:
x <- 200.8  # numeric
y <- 1000L  # integer
z <- 1i     # complex
You can convert from one type to another with the following functions:
as.numeric()
as.integer()
as.complex()
Try these in the sandbox below:
x <- 200.8  # numeric
y <- 1000L  # integer

x2 <- as.integer(x) #what happens here?

y2 <- as.numeric(y) #what happens here?

class(x2)

class(y2)

title: 01. R, Rstudio: Crash Course
text:
Vectors
A vector is simply a list of items that are of the same type.
To combine the list of items to a vectowebr-r, use the c() function and separate the items by a comma.
In the example below, we create a vector variable called planets, that combines strings:
#vector of strings

planets <- c("Earth", "Mars", "Saturn")

#print planets
planets
In this example, we create a vector that combines numerical values:
#vector of numeric values

prime_numbers<- c(2, 3, 5, 7, 11)

#print prime numbers

prime_numbers
You can create a sequence of numbers using : :
Vector with numerical values in a sequence:
numbers <- 1:10

numbers

title: 1.1.Statistics and Samples
text:
Learning Goals

Understand the major goals of statistics
Understand the distinction between the term “population” in a statistical and a biological context.
Distinguish between a sample and a population
Distinguish between an estimate and a parameter
Identify why estimates from samples may deviate from parameters of populations

These learning goals are for the entire topic/unit. They will also be available in the study guide.

title: 1.1.Statistics and Samples
text:
Statistics deals with UNCERTAINTY

Statistics are a quantitative technology for empirical science.
A logic and methodology for the measurement of uncertainty and for an examination of that uncertainty.
The key word here is uncertainty. Statistics becomes necessary when observations are variable.

title: 1.1.Statistics and Samples
text:
Populations & Samples

In Statistics, a population is the entire collection of individual units that a researcher is interested in. E.g. all women born in the US between 1990 and 200; all polar bears currently living in zoos; users of a certain social network in a certain age group; etc


A sample is a subset of these units that we collect and measure.

title: 1.1.Statistics and Samples
text:
Statistics & Parameters (1/3)
A parameter is some property of the world, i.e., the “truth”.

Decorative image. Poster from the show “The X-files”

title: 1.1.Statistics and Samples
text:
Statistics & Parameters (2/3)

Because we can’t sample an entire population, we usually don’t know parameters. Parameters describe Populations.
But we can get a good sense of the parameters from estimates we make from Samples.
Estimates (statistics) approximate parameters as inferred from Samples.

title: 1.1.Statistics and Samples
text:
Statistics & Parameters (3/3)

Parameters are constants. This means that they are fixed. Parameters represent the world. Parameters are the truth.
Estimates are “random variables”. This means estimates change from one random sample to the next from the same population.

title: 1.1.Statistics and Samples
text:
A population of starfish



Parameters describe populations
E.g. proportion of pink starfish among all starfish of a given species in a certain location

title: 1.1.Statistics and Samples
text:
A sample of starfish



Estimates (statistics) approximate parameters as inferred from samples.
We estimate the proportion of pink as inferred from this sample and extrapolate to the population as an approximation.
